narrative: The model estimates a 17% probability that you will fail your final year. That is a low risk estimate, so the requirement for remedial courses is best understood as a precautionary step rather than a strong forecast that you are likely to fail. The three most influential factors were your past class failures, your father’s education, and your intention to pursue higher education. Importantly, each of these pushed the prediction toward passing, not failing. Your record of no past class failures matches the average for students who passed and was the strongest protective factor. Your father having completed higher education was also protective, even though only about one in four passing students had a father at that level. Your wish to continue to higher education was the third protective factor; all passing students in the comparison group shared that goal, and you do too. Because the leading factors reduce risk, the low failure probability is consistent. To improve further, keep your weekly study time at two to five hours or more, maintain full attendance, use family support, and treat remedial courses as an opportunity to strengthen weaker areas rather than as proof you are expected to fail.
